reviewed_entry.definition: A preparatory response is a temporary increase in general alertness or readiness that occurs when an event is expected, especially at a predictable time, and facilitates responding at that moment.

packet.text:
signal before target presentation, and the typical finding is that the warning signal speeds responses by elevating general readiness (e.g., Hackley, 2009 ; Posner and Boies, 1971 ; Petersen and Posner, 2012 ; Schneider, 2019 ). Past studies have demonstrated that temporal warning signals that specify when something is about to appear produce alerting benefits. These benefits are typically expressed as faster RT, but sometimes at the expense of reduced accuracy, depending on the reliability of the cue and observers’ expectations ( Han and Proctor, 2022 , 2023 ; Lawrence and Klein, 2013 ). While the tasks examining external warning signals and PE are different, they share a common underlying mechanism of temporal preparation: in both paradigms, the observer uses learned temporal regularities (i.e., when events reliably occur) to boost nonspecific, general-purpose alerting readiness at the expected moment.

It seems, therefore, that the PE is an instance of a more general alerting mechanism: when an event is expected at a fixed time, the system enters a high-alert, process-all mode, boosting general readiness at the anticipated moment rather than selectively filtering or suppressing processing. In light of previous findings demonstrating the rigidity of the PE, the goal of the current study was to identify its boundary conditions (if any). That is, understanding when this preparatory response holds and when it might be attenuated or absent will allow us to better characterize the underlying mechanism of the PE and relate it to other temporal attention mechanisms.

Experiment 1 tested whether the preparation benefit in the PE paradigm is sensitive to the probability of an event occurring, as is the case with other phasic alertness phenomena ( Los et al., 2014 ). Experiment 2 examined whether the PE holds even after participants gain extensive practice or whether it habituates over time, as was found in other preparatory paradigms ( Cunningham and Egeth, 2016 ). Experiment 3 tested whether the PE benefit persists when the probe is defined by other stimulus attributes and not by an abrupt onset. That is, we asked whether a preparation benefit would emerge even when observers are asked to detect an offset event (i.e., “something disappearing”) instead of an onset event (i.e., “dot appearing”). This will clarify the role of attentional set ( Folk et al., 1992 ) in modulating the effect and, more broadly, will address the question of whether phasic alertness is specifically tied to onset detection.

In sum, although the PE was found to be robust, it is important to consider its limitations and the boundary conditions of this effect. This would help clarify whether the PE reflects a general-purpose mechanism of attentional preparation that operates rigidly across a range of conditions, or whether it depends on specific contextual factors that may limit its generalizability.
packet.source_label: On the rigidity of the preparation effect

Choose the primary field of the HEADWORD'S PSYCHOLOGY MEANING from the 14 definitions below, using only the packet and its actual source label/aliases. Do not copy an inherited field or classify by the article's subject, venue or laboratory location. Classify the term's meaning. This is taxonomy assignment, not a second eligibility/scope decision. counselling skills: Therapeutic communication, counselling techniques and the practitioner-client relationship.
assessment: Psychological measurement, tests, screening, scoring and interpretation of individual functioning.
diagnosis: Classification and identification of mental or developmental disorders and diagnostic concepts.
ethics: Professional duties, consent, confidentiality, boundaries and responsible psychological practice.
development: Psychological and behavioural change across the lifespan, including attachment and developmental processes.
cognition: Perception, attention, memory, language, reasoning, judgement and other mental information processes.
social: How social interactions, relationships, groups and culture shape thought, feeling and behaviour.
biological: Neural, hormonal or genetic mechanisms explicitly connected to psychological or behavioural functioning.
research methods: Study design, sampling, statistics, evidence evaluation and methodological concepts used in psychological research.
history: Historical schools, theories and concepts whose historical identity is central to their meaning.
mental health: Psychological wellbeing, distress, symptoms, prevention and care that are not chiefly diagnostic classification.
learning: Conditioning, reinforcement, skill acquisition, education and changes in behaviour or knowledge through experience.
personality: Enduring individual differences, traits, temperament, character and theories of personality.
emotion and motivation: Affective states, emotion regulation, drives, goals, needs and processes energising behaviour.

{"headword": "preparatory response", "taxonomy_hint": "cognition", "source_packet": {"headword": "preparatory response", "field": "cognition", "source": "article-pmc13350337", "source_record": "10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1787472", "revision": "2026; DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1787472; article XML SHA-256 850aa239dc1410413d8cbda0bb8225ec14bb0ba937065ed81a1d92804675b0d1", "text": "signal before target presentation, and the typical finding is that the warning signal speeds responses by elevating general readiness (e.g., Hackley, 2009 ; Posner and Boies, 1971 ; Petersen and Posner, 2012 ; Schneider, 2019 ). Past studies have demonstrated that temporal warning signals that specify when something is about to appear produce alerting benefits. These benefits are typically expressed as faster RT, but sometimes at the expense of reduced accuracy, depending on the reliability of the cue and observers’ expectations ( Han and Proctor, 2022 , 2023 ; Lawrence and Klein, 2013 ). While the tasks examining external warning signals and PE are different, they share a common underlying mechanism of temporal preparation: in both paradigms, the observer uses learned temporal regularities (i.e., when events reliably occur) to boost nonspecific, general-purpose alerting readiness at the expected moment.

It seems, therefore, that the PE is an instance of a more general alerting mechanism: when an event is expected at a fixed time, the system enters a high-alert, process-all mode, boosting general readiness at the anticipated moment rather than selectively filtering or suppressing processing. In light of previous findings demonstrating the rigidity of the PE, the goal of the current study was to identify its boundary conditions (if any). That is, understanding when this preparatory response holds and when it might be attenuated or absent will allow us to better characterize the underlying mechanism of the PE and relate it to other temporal attention mechanisms.

Experiment 1 tested whether the preparation benefit in the PE paradigm is sensitive to the probability of an event occurring, as is the case with other phasic alertness phenomena ( Los et al., 2014 ). Experiment 2 examined whether the PE holds even after participants gain extensive practice or whether it habituates over time, as was found in other preparatory paradigms ( Cunningham and Egeth, 2016 ). Experiment 3 tested whether the PE benefit persists when the probe is defined by other stimulus attributes and not by an abrupt onset. That is, we asked whether a preparation benefit would emerge even when observers are asked to detect an offset event (i.e., “something disappearing”) instead of an onset event (i.e., “dot appearing”). This will clarify the role of attentional set ( Folk et al., 1992 ) in modulating the effect and, more broadly, will address the question of whether phasic alertness is specifically tied to onset detection.

In sum, although the PE was found to be robust, it is important to consider its limitations and the boundary conditions of this effect. This would help clarify whether the PE reflects a general-purpose mechanism of attentional preparation that operates rigidly across a range of conditions, or whether it depends on specific contextual factors that may limit its generalizability.", "source_record_label": "On the rigidity of the preparation effect", "publisher_aliases": []}, "draft_to_check": {"definition": "A preparatory response is a temporary increase in general alertness or readiness that occurs when an event is expected, especially at a predictable time, and facilitates responding at that moment."}}

counselling skills: Therapeutic communication, counselling techniques and the practitioner-client relationship.
assessment: Psychological measurement, tests, screening, scoring and interpretation of individual functioning.
diagnosis: Classification and identification of mental or developmental disorders and diagnostic concepts.
ethics: Professional duties, consent, confidentiality, boundaries and responsible psychological practice.
development: Psychological and behavioural change across the lifespan, including attachment and developmental processes.
cognition: Perception, attention, memory, language, reasoning, judgement and other mental information processes.
social: How social interactions, relationships, groups and culture shape thought, feeling and behaviour.
biological: Neural, hormonal or genetic mechanisms explicitly connected to psychological or behavioural functioning.
research methods: Study design, sampling, statistics, evidence evaluation and methodological concepts used in psychological research.
history: Historical schools, theories and concepts whose historical identity is central to their meaning.
mental health: Psychological wellbeing, distress, symptoms, prevention and care that are not chiefly diagnostic classification.
learning: Conditioning, reinforcement, skill acquisition, education and changes in behaviour or knowledge through experience.
personality: Enduring individual differences, traits, temperament, character and theories of personality.
emotion and motivation: Affective states, emotion regulation, drives, goals, needs and processes energising behaviour.
